news.title: Scammers Can Fake Your Grandchild's Voice Now — Here's the Family Fix
news.excerpt: Scammers are calling grandparents in a voice that sounds exactly like their grandchild — because a computer cloned it. The Better Business Bureau warned families this week, just before Grandparents' Day: crooks lift a few seconds of audio and family details from social media, then fake a crash or an arrest and beg for money fast. Hang up and call your grandchild back yourself, and set up a family code word. Then lock your Facebook photos to friends-only — that's where they shop for voices.

news.title: Scammers Posing as Microsoft Support Are After Your Password — Hang Up
news.excerpt: Microsoft issued a warning Friday: crooks are calling people while pretending to be the computer's support team — sometimes claiming to be Microsoft — saying your account needs an urgent "security update." Then they text you a link to a sign-in page that looks exactly like the real one. Real Microsoft never calls first. Hang up, delete the text, and if you already typed your password, change it now — then call me.

news.title: Letters Went Out to 4.1 Million Patients This Week — Expect the Scam Calls Too
news.excerpt: Letters are arriving this week for 4.1 million customers of AdaptHealth — the company that delivers home medical equipment like sleep apnea and oxygen machines. Thieves stole names, health details, and insurance information. Scammers buy lists like this fast, so expect calls offering to "help you claim free credit monitoring." If you get a letter, use only the phone number printed on it — never one a caller gives you. And glance over your insurance statements for care you never received.

news.title: The Biggest Windows Security Update Ever Went Out Tuesday — Install It Tonight
news.excerpt: Microsoft just shipped its biggest security update ever — nearly 1,000 fixes in a single day, and two of the holes being patched were already under attack. If your computer hasn't updated since Tuesday, it's missing protection against bugs criminals are using right now. Updating takes a few minutes, then restart when it asks. Put it off and you're leaving the door unlocked. Do it tonight.

news.title: That 'Unpaid Ticket' Text Is a Scam — Delete It, Don't Tap It
news.excerpt: A wave of fake "DMV" text messages is hitting drivers across the country right now — texts claiming your license will be suspended for an unpaid ticket and demanding payment through a link. Florida's own DMV says it will NEVER text you demanding money or threatening suspension. If you tap the link, you hand your card to criminals. Delete the text, don't reply, and report it by forwarding to 7726.

posts.title: Your LG TV reports what you watch to advertisers — turn it off free in Settings > General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus
posts.summary: A new investigation put it back in the news this week: LG smart TVs record a fingerprint of everything you watch — cable, streaming, even over-the-air — and send it home so advertisers can target you. The fix is one free switch, no account needed: press the Settings (gear) button on the remote, go to General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus, and turn it off. On Samsung TVs the similar switch lives under Settings > General > Terms & Privacy.
posts.truth: Here's the one that surprises everybody: the TV is a computer, and the biggest screen in the house is also the chattiest. Someone buying a television based on selling your viewing habits — what time you watch, what channel, whether it's football or the news — and you'd never know it, because it never asks twice. The honest answer is I'm not saying smash your TV; I'm saying a six-hundred-dollar TV doesn't need a second income. Two minutes with the remote and it goes back to being just a TV. The picture doesn't change one bit. You'll never miss the setting, and neither will the advertisers — they're the only ones who lose.

posts.title: Update Chrome, VLC, Zoom, and a dozen apps in one click — Ninite is free at ninite.com
posts.summary: Go to ninite.com, check the boxes for the free apps you already use — Chrome, Firefox, VLC, Zoom, and dozens more — and it builds you one installer. Run it once and Ninite installs or updates everything together; no toolbars, no junk offers. Keep that one file on your desktop, run it again about once a month, and every app on the list refreshes itself. Free for home use.
posts.truth: Here's the part almost nobody believes: your computer doesn't usually get broken by viruses walking in the front door — it gets broken by old programs standing in the back doorway. Criminals poke at well-known free apps that haven't been updated in a year, because the maker already published the fix and you just haven't gotten it. Updating twelve apps by hand is a Saturday morning you don't have. The honest answer is there's a website built for exactly this problem, it's been around for well over a decade, and it refuses to bundle junk — that refusal is the whole reason I trust it. One click, one download, one run, and the sneaky back doors close.

posts.title: Is someone in your email right now? Check your Sent folder, then open your account's recent activity page to see every device that signed in
posts.summary: Check your Sent folder for messages you never wrote, then open your email provider's recent-activity page to see every device that has signed in: for Gmail it's myaccount.google.com/security, for Outlook or Hotmail it's account.microsoft.com/security. Anything you don't recognize means it's time to change your password — or come see me.
posts.truth: Here's the trick I wish every customer knew: when crooks break into an email, they don't leave a note — but they do leave footprints. Almost every email account keeps a list of every device that signed in, where it was, and when, and almost nobody ever looks at it. The honest answer is the "weird thing" people notice — friends saying you sent them a strange link, a password reset email they never asked for — is usually the third or fourth clue, not the first. Two minutes in that activity list and you'll know for sure. Most of the time it's just you, your phone, and your tablet, and you'll sleep better.

posts.title: Your scanner needs its disc back? NAPS2 is the free download at naps2.com that makes any scanner work on a fresh computer
posts.summary: NAPS2 (short for "Not Another PDF Scanner 2") is completely free scanner software — download it at naps2.com, click Install, and it works with HP, Canon, Epson, and Brother scanners, saving scans straight to searchable PDFs. No manufacturer disc, no account, no ads.
posts.truth: I see this all the time: somebody gets a new computer, dusts off their scanner, and spends an hour hunting for the installation disc that came with it eight years ago. The scanner itself is fine — the disc was just the key. The honest answer is you don't need the disc or the manufacturer's bloated software suite that wants to run ten things at startup. NAPS2 is what I install on my own shop scanner: it's small, it's free, and it turns a stack of receipts, insurance papers, or old family photos into tidy PDFs with one button. Most people don't realize "it doesn't work anymore" usually just means "it never got installed."

posts.title: Chrome now updates every two weeks — check yours free in the Chrome menu under About Google Chrome
posts.summary: Google switched Google Chrome to a two-week update schedule as of September 8, which means the security fixes arrive twice as often — open Chrome, click the three-dot menu in the top corner, choose Help > About Google Chrome, and it checks and updates itself for free in under a minute.
posts.truth: Here's something that changed this week and most people will never hear about: Chrome, the browser half of Lake City uses, now updates every two weeks instead of every four. Google did it because the bad guys are using the same AI tools we are, and holes get found — and used — faster. The honest answer is you don't have to understand any of that. The trick is knowing your browser updates itself while it's open — an old update just sits there waiting if you haven't restarted Chrome in a month. One click in the menu, and it's done.

posts.title: Microsoft just sealed 974 security holes in one day — the update is free, here's how to confirm you got it
posts.summary: Open Settings > Windows Update on your PC and click Check for updates — Microsoft released its biggest security update ever on September 9, covering 974 holes in Windows, including ones criminals were already using. It's free, it's built into Windows, and it takes about ten minutes.
posts.truth: Here's a number that surprised even me: 974. That's how many security holes Microsoft patched in a single day this week — their biggest patch release ever. Most people don't realize that when your computer asks to "restart to finish updating," it isn't nagging you for fun; it's locking the doors behind you. The honest answer is you don't need to understand what any of those holes are. You just need to let Windows close them. The folks who get in trouble are the ones who keep clicking "remind me later" for months.

posts.title: Rapid Fiber Internet is done building — every Suwannee Valley Electric member can now get fiber internet; check your address at svec-coop.com
posts.summary: Suwannee Valley Electric's Rapid Fiber Internet finished its $93 million build this month — true fiber internet is now available to all of SVEC's members across our area. Check your address free at svec-coop.com/rapid-fiber-internet, or call SVEC at 800-447-4509 to ask when your home can connect.
posts.truth: I've heard "the internet out here is just slow" so many times that folks stopped asking why. The honest answer is it was never your computer — out in the country around Lake City, most connections travel miles of old copper lines that were never built for video calls and streaming. Rapid Fiber spent the last four years burying brand-new fiber lines past more than 28,000 homes, and they finished the job this month. If you've been paying for sluggish internet and blaming yourself, check that map. Fiber means video calls that don't freeze, movies that don't buffer, and one less thing between your family and the rest of the world.

posts.title: That old Windows computer your kid outgrew? Google's free ChromeOS Flex gives it a second life as a fast, simple Chromebook
posts.summary: Google offers ChromeOS Flex completely free at chromeos.google/products/chromeos-flex — download it to a USB stick, plug it into your old Windows computer, and it becomes a fast, safe Chromebook-style machine that starts up in seconds and updates itself automatically.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize the slow part of an old computer is usually the aging Windows setup, not the machine itself. Google's free program wipes that old system and replaces it with the same quick, simple software Chromebooks run — web, email, photos, YouTube, all just there, and it updates itself so there's nothing to manage. The honest answer is it's not for everyone: it won't run Windows programs like QuickBooks desktop, and that's a dealbreaker for some folks. But for the kitchen computer that only ever opened a browser anyway, it's the difference between the closet and the counter — without spending a dime.
